title: The moths and the lamp
hook: insects flying into the oil lamps at night

segments.voice: Yesterday: the elephant read whole, and your line, each held a part. Did you let someone finish before you decided? Today, one of the shortest scenes in the Udana. Day six hundred twenty.

Sit on a porch on a summer night with the light on, and you'll see it. Moths come out of the dark, circle the bulb, bump it, circle again. With an electric bulb they mostly just get tired. With a candle or an oil lamp, it's different. They fly into the flame, and that's the end of them. Nobody really knows, even now, exactly why moths do it; scientists are still arguing about it. The Udana doesn't try to explain the moths. It just watches them. Today: the moths and the lamp.
screen: `A PORCH LIGHT ON A SUMMER NIGHT.` → `A FLAME IS DIFFERENT.` → `THE UDANA JUST WATCHES.`

segments.voice: The whole story takes a few lines. The Buddha is sitting outdoors in the dark of the night, and oil lamps are burning. Many winged insects are flying around them, and falling into the lamps, one after another, to their harm, to their ruin. The Buddha sees this. And, knowing the meaning of it, he speaks the verse. Rushing up, passing by what's essential, they bring on new bonds again and again, like insects falling into a lamp. So some are bound up in what is seen and heard. That's all. No crowd, no question, no long teaching. A man sitting in the dark, watching. And notice the word in the middle: passing by what's essential. The moths aren't stupid. They're drawn by something real, the light. The trouble is that they mistake the light for something it isn't, and they keep coming back. The verse says people can do the same with the seen and the heard, the bright thing on the screen, the voice that pulls us, rushing to it again and again, each time tying another knot. There's a link back to Bahiya, a few days ago: in the seen, only the seen. The moth doesn't stop at the seen. It flies straight in. And there's something tender in the scene, too. The Buddha doesn't scold the moths. He watches them in the night, and sees us.
screen: `OIL LAMPS BURNING IN THE DARK.` · `FALLING IN, ONE AFTER ANOTHER.` · `PASSING BY WHAT'S ESSENTIAL.` · `BOUND BY THE SEEN AND THE HEARD.` · then, large: `THE MOTHS AND THE FLAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one flame you fly into. Sit and settle. Ask: what bright thing do I keep circling, even when it burns a little? A feed, a fight, a craving, a particular kind of evening that always ends the same way. Picture it as a lamp in the dark. Watch yourself circling it, with kindness, the way the Buddha watched the moths. You don't have to stop yet. Just see the circling. The bell holds the time.
The moths and the lamp. In the Udana, insects falling into oil lamps at night: the picture of rushing again and again to the seen and the heard. Today's word.
screen: `THE MOTHS AND THE LAMP — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the moths and the flame. Today, when you feel the pull toward your bright thing, pause one breath before you fly in. Day six hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Teachers in many Buddhist traditions use the image of moths and a flame for craving that harms the one who craves, and the Udana's scene is often read at evening talks.

fork.setup: you're sitting outdoors at night and moths are falling into the oil lamps, one after another. what does the Buddha do in the Udana?
options: watch, and speak a verse about people bound to the seen and heard.
fork.reveal: the text says only that he saw, and spoke the verse. the scene is short, and it's about us as much as the moths.

original.note: Pali patanga: a winged insect, a moth. the insects fall into the lamps in Udana 6.9.

trapdoor: what you thought: moths are drawn to light because they're foolish.
what it means: they're drawn by something real, and mistake it; the verse says people do the same with the seen and the heard.
what a scholar hears: Udana 6.9 uses the rare word patanga and ties the image to new bonds (bandhanani) of the seen and heard; the moth and flame also appear in Indian poetry for desire.
